title: Stopped at the top: is it still pulled?
hook: At the top of its flight the ball stops for an instant. Has gravity stopped too?

knows: a ball thrown up slows, stops and falls back
doesNotKnow: that acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a different thing from velocity
that the acceleration of a thrown ball is g downward throughout its flight

misconception: At the top, where the speed is zero, the acceleration is zero too.
objective: The learner can explain that at the top the velocity is zero but still changing, from up to down, so the acceleration is 9.81 m/s^2 downward at every instant, including the top.

claims.text: With no air resistance, a thrown ball's acceleration is 9.81 m/s² downward at every point of its flight, including the top.
claims.source: The only force is weight m g, so a = -g throughout (Newton's second law). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 2.9 (free-fall acceleration).

claims.text: Thrown up at 14.7 m/s, the ball reaches the top after 1.50 s, 11.0 m up.
claims.source: t = v0 / g = 14.7 / 9.81 = 1.498 s; h = v0^2 / (2 g) = 11.01 m. Checked by numerical integration (dt = 1e-5 s): peak 1.4985 s, 11.01 m.

claims.text: Its velocity is v = 14.7 − 9.81 t: +1.95 m/s (up) at 1.3 s, +0.97 m/s at 1.4 s, about zero (−0.02 m/s) at 1.5 s and −1.00 m/s (down) at 1.6 s. It drops by 0.98 m/s every 0.1 s (9.81 m/s every second), before the top, through it and after; the reveal quotes the latest upward and earliest downward times the learner visited.
claims.source: v = 14.7 - 9.81 t: 14.7 - 13.734 = 0.966 m/s; 14.7 - 15.696 = -0.996 m/s. The stage computes v(t) at 0.1 s steps from 0 to 2.9 s; checked in node. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node: v(1.3) = 1.947, v(1.4) = 0.966, v(1.5) = -0.015, v(1.6) = -0.996, shown by signed() as +1.95, +0.97, −0.02, −1.00; every 0.1 s step from 0 to 2.9 s drops v by 0.981 (DV shown as 0.98). Reveal takes max of visited ups (v > 0.05) and min of downs (v < -0.05).

claims.text: If the acceleration were zero at the top, the ball would stay hanging in the air, because its velocity would stop changing.
claims.source: a = dv/dt; with v = 0 and a = 0 the velocity stays 0 (Newton's first law). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own derivation: a = dv/dt, and the force on the ball depends only on its state (position, velocity). If that force were zero at the top state (v = 0), staying at the top would solve the equation of motion, and by uniqueness it would be the motion: the velocity stops changing and the ball hangs. Reveal sentence matches the claim.

claims.text: The lesson ignores air resistance; with air, the acceleration at the top is still 9.81 m/s² down, because drag is zero when the ball is at rest.
claims.source: Stated on stage ('No air.') and in the reveal. Drag depends on speed (F = 1/2 rho C_d A v^2) and vanishes at v = 0, leaving only m g at the top.

recall.question: A juggler's ball hangs motionless for an instant at the top of its arc. At that instant, the ball's acceleration is…
recall.why: Zero velocity is not zero acceleration: the velocity is changing from up to down at 9.81 m/s every second, so gravity's acceleration never pauses.
